Question
========
Suppose you have a large sample from a smooth, roughly normal variable. If you increase the number of bins in a
histogram of this variable from a small number (e.g., 5) to a very large number (e.g., 200), what generally happens to
the histogram's appearance?

Answerlist
----------
* It becomes progressively smoother, revealing an increasingly clear and simple shape.
* It becomes more jagged, with bin-to-bin fluctuations caused by having only a few observations per bin.
* Its shape reverses, so a right-skewed distribution appears left-skewed.
* Its appearance stays exactly the same, since only bin width changes, not the underlying data.

Solution
========

Answerlist
----------
* Wrong: more bins means fewer observations per bin, which introduces more random noise, not less.
* Correct: with very many bins, each bin contains very few observations, so bar heights become noisy and jagged.
* Wrong: increasing the number of bins does not change which side of the distribution has the longer tail.
* Wrong: the number of bins directly changes how the data are grouped, so the plot's appearance does change.
